![The elite women's lead pack at a TCS marathon. Image from [Runner's World](https://www.runnersworld.com/uk/training/a71879504/how-to-mimic-elite-runner-mechanics/).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Runner's World](https://www.runnersworld.com/uk/training/a71879504/how-to-mimic-elite-runner-mechanics/) collects the biomechanics research on why elite runners look effortless, and it makes a claim I find more useful than the usual "run more" advice: the gap is mostly about where the propulsive force comes from and how little time the foot spends on the ground, rather than raw fitness.

The article's account of the elite–amateur gap breaks into four linked mechanisms, in the order the piece presents them:

- **Propulsion originates in the calves.** [Scott Delp](https://profiles.stanford.edu/scott-delp) (Stanford bioengineering) names the gastrocnemius and soleus as the biggest contributors to upward and forward propulsion, working through plantar flexion. A 2023 *Frontiers in Sports and Active Living* study found trained collegiate runners drew more of their power from the ankle than recreational runners, tracking with their faster speeds. In slower runners the knee does more of the work, so the quads dominate push-off, and quad-driven push-off adds a horizontal force directed backward that decelerates. The prescription is targeted calf work: calf raises and their variations.

- **Faster runners spend less time on the ground.** [Mike Hahn](https://bssc.uoregon.edu/) (University of Oregon) frames speed as the ability to exert force against the ground more quickly. A 2022 *Bioengineering* study found elite and experienced runners have a lower "duty factor," less time with the foot down, while older work in the *Journal of Applied Physiology* found faster runners apply about 1.26 times the average ground force. A deep knee bend and ankle dorsiflexion make for a soft, spongy stride that wastes energy stabilizing the body. Shortening step length and raising cadence lands the foot under the body and gets it off the ground faster.

- **A stiff ankle behaves like a spring.** A 2023 *Frontiers in Physiology* study found elites run "springier." On landing, a stiff ankle stores and returns elastic energy, while a floppy one acts as a shock absorber and loses that return as the runner sinks into the quads. Plyometrics such as pogo jumps are cited as a proven way to build tendon stiffness.

- **The payoff is a longer aerial phase.** A study in the *European Journal of Sport Science* compared elites and recreational runners at the same speed and found the main difference was neither stride length nor cadence but an 11% longer flight time. Elites dip less on landing and hold a higher, longer push-off, like a bouncing ball with a shallow dip and a pronounced rise. The article presents air time as the cumulative result of the other three mechanisms, earned through consistent training.
